data.signal: Hurlston pushed back on the assumption that Lumentum OCS equals Google: 'the breadth of customer engagement is very high on OCS. We started with customers other than Google... we actually have customers that were much more substantial than Google in our early rounds of shipments.' One of the more interesting emerging use cases is deploying an OCS inside the rack itself, one per rack, to route around GPUs or TPUs that have failed or are overloaded - a surprising number of GPUs in a data center fail, and a compute model can represent '$20, 30, $40 million of compute time'. At the lead customer the number of OCSs per torus is also going up. data.signal: New EML economics and share math. Moving from 100G to 200G EML gives 'about a 2x uplift in price' - ASPs roughly double - and 200G lasers arrive at the 1.6T node. At 200G there is 'very little competition': Broadcom is a supplier of 200G EMLs, Lumentum is the other large supplier, and management sees no other entrants soon. On mix, EML-based transceivers are 'probably 70%-80%' of the 800G market but are expected to be only '40%-50% of the market at 1.6T' as silicon photonics takes share, so raw EML units go up while share comes down. At 3.2T Lumentum's transceiver engineers say 'silicon photonics again runs out of steam', producing 'a double whammy' where both EML unit numbers and EML share rise. Hurlston also framed the yield argument behind the price premium: the tolerance of the laser sets transceiver yield more than anything else, so a higher laser price 'more than makes up for itself in the high yields'.

At the 1.6T transition Lumentum got to the head of the curve on signal integrity and is 'now shipping ahead of great competitors like InnoLight and Coherent' (Eoptolink also named), first to market on a lot of its SKUs. The unresolved problem is gross margin - still below the top competitors - which management plans to attack on the manufacturing side entering calendar 2027, while conceding it may never match InnoLight or Eoptolink.

It seems like now it's a late 2027 into early 2028 event', because customers competing with NVIDIA concluded they need to deploy a lot more optics and to do so sooner. Hurlston called the near-term NPO opportunity larger than the CPO opportunity, with a higher adoption rate of optical lanes than NVIDIA's, and said NPO customers are requiring Lumentum to ship the entire ELS rather than bare laser chips. The consequence is capacity: NPO 'is going to put a lot of pressure on that Greensboro fab', Lumentum needs a 'next leg of the stool' and is trying to lock up NPO business now to fill Greensboro and more, but would require an NVIDIA-style commitment before funding further capacity. NVIDIA underwrote Greensboro with a long-term agreement characterised as a multibillion-dollar deal plus an investment that helped Lumentum buy, equip and outfit the fab, acquired early calendar 2026 and not operational until early calendar 2028; the team running it was inherited from Qorvo, and qualification at NVIDIA itself took a year.

The reverse risk is tit-for-tat curtailment of Chinese sub-component supply - substrates, isolators and other raw materials Lumentum currently relies on - against which its manufacturing footprint in Thailand, in China itself and in the United Kingdom (a safe harbour on substrates) is the hedge.

data.signal: Kathy Ta sized the optical bandwidth step-up per interconnect tier for the first time: if Data Center Interconnect / telecom is a 1x multiple, scale-across and scale-out are each roughly 10x DCI; the first instance of CPO going to scale-up, starting in the second half of 2027, is 'probably 3x to 4x above the 10x that we are seeing for scale-out', and when all of scale-up goes optical it is 'a full 10x above the 10x of scale-out', with scale-in another 10x multiple beyond that. Wupen Yuen framed the same ladder as scale-across 1, scale-out 10, scale-up 100, scale-in 1,000, and positioned Lumentum as 'going all the way from scale across to scale out, to scale up, and later to scale in'.

data.signal: Post-earnings supply update: the supply-demand gap is 'still extending' and Lumentum is 'still short everywhere' - DML short, CW laser short. Yuen does not see the shortage going away in 2027; the industry forecasts scale-out module volume doubling from 2026 to 2027 while laser supply does not catch up, and 2028 scale-up drives another 3 to 4x increase of demand, so the laser supply-demand gap does not close within the next couple of years. Lumentum is still allocating capacity, in some cases on pricing and expedite fees, to serve the most profitable opportunities, and 'all the deals we are making today are equal or higher pricing than the escalated pricing that we already had before' - management's own read that the gap persists.
data.figure: scale-out module volume doubling from 2026 to 2027; 2028 scale-up drives another 3 to 4x demand increase; gap does not close within the next couple of years

data.signal: Yuen reframed optical scale-up as an industry-wide story rather than the single-customer CPO story assumed at OFC: to serve 2028 optical scale-up volume the industry needs both CPO and NPO approaches, and by volume 'CPO will be half of the market. NPO is the other half of the market' - roughly 50/50. On the content Lumentum sells, CPO is 'an exclusive external light source market'; half of NPO also goes external light source (ELS) and the remaining roughly 25% of the overall market is still being debated between integrated light source (ILS) and ELS, with more and more movement toward ELS because the optical engine sits so close to the accelerator heat source that an integrated laser becomes the reliability-limiting factor. Even the ILS case will not use pluggable-class lasers: an NPO engine '1 inch by half an inch' packs 6.4T versus half an iPhone for a 1.6T module today, so fewer but higher-power lasers are required and the entire NPO/CPO application moves to '120, 150 milliwatt and above', not the traditional 70 milliwatt pluggable laser. Chinese CW laser supply chatter is aimed at that pluggable market, not this one.
data.figure: CPO half and NPO half of the optical scale-up market; ILS about 25% of the overall market; NPO engine 1 inch by half an inch packing 6.4T vs a 1.6T module today; 120, 150 milliwatt and above vs traditional 70 milliwatt

He described why the part is hard (power, RIN noise, linewidth and mode hop all have to be achieved simultaneously at volume with good yield, and mode hop is the biggest problem with today's silicon photonics lasers), noted Lumentum is already ramping these lasers and seeing good real data, and then said the industry needs a second source: from a customer's point of view Coherent would need to be ramping 'sometime in 2027... Probably second half' to support the scale-up build in 2028.

data.signal: CONTRACTED LOAD ADDITIONS REACH 69 GIGAWATTS through 2030, up six gigawatts from the 63 GW disclosed last quarter — 'AEP contracted an additional six gigawatts of load, primarily driven by fully executed LOAs in Texas.' All of it is supported by fully executed ESAs and LOAs that require customers to secure land, complete interconnection studies, provide detailed load forecasts and fund the associated infrastructure investments. Geographic split: Texas 45 GW, Ohio 12 GW, and Oklahoma, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana and Virginia combined 12 GW. Management stresses counterparty quality — 'the vast majority of these projects are being advanced by well-capitalized hyperscalers and large industrial customers with significant financial resources.' Executed LOAs and ESAs have increased every quarter for the last six to seven quarters.
data.figure: 69 GW contracted load through 2030 (up 6 GW from 63 GW last quarter); Texas 45 GW, Ohio 12 GW, other states 12 GW

data.signal: AEP TEXAS SUBMITTED 45 GIGAWATTS OF PROJECTS INTO ERCOT'S BATCH ZERO process, forecast between now and 2032, with ERCOT expected to determine eligibility on August 7. The credit support is already in hand: 'just over the past month, we have collected nearly $2 billion in cash or collateral for load commitments in ERCOT, which represents all the required credit support for the full 45 gigawatts included in AEP Texas's Batch Zero filing.' Of the 205 gigawatts ERCOT published as eligible for Batch Zero, AEP is 'roughly, call it, a quarter of that', and the CFO treats its 45 GW as firm — a worst case only slips projects from Batch Zero to Batch One. Critical for the equipment chain: the $78 billion capital plan assumed only about 13 gigawatts of interconnection in Texas and 'does not anticipate this magnitude of load growth', and there is 'almost 100 gigawatts in Texas behind that 45 gigawatts', with 195 gigawatts of parties actively trying to interconnect to the queue.
data.figure: 45 GW submitted to ERCOT Batch Zero (out of 205 GW eligible); nearly $2 billion of cash/collateral posted; $78B plan assumed only about 13 GW of Texas interconnection; almost 100 GW more queued behind it; 195 GW in the interconnection queue

data.signal: FIVE-YEAR CAPITAL PLAN OF $78 BILLION for 2026 through 2030, expected to result in nearly 11% rate base CAGR — 'AEP's five-year capital plan stood at just $38 billion only four years ago.' Beyond the base plan the company has 'line of sight to over $10 billion of incremental investments that are not included in the $78 billion, consisting of the fuel cells for the Wyoming project, the Piketon transmission opportunity, and incremental power generation.' A new 2027 to 2031 plan will be introduced on the third-quarter earnings call, with the secured generation investments expected to be an important driver of the long-term growth outlook. Financing for the base plan is de-risked: a $3 billion marketed equity transaction settled under forward contracts by May 2028 addresses all anticipated marketed equity needs, with a targeted FFO to debt ratio of 14% to 15%.
data.figure: $78B five-year capital plan 2026-2030 (nearly 11% rate base CAGR), up from $38B four years ago; over $10B of identified incremental investment outside the plan

data.signal: TURBINE SUPPLY IS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT AND AEP IS PRE-BUYING IT: an additional three gigawatts of gas-fired turbines secured during the quarter takes total secured turbine capacity to approximately 13 gigawatts for deployment through 2031, and AEP is 'leveraging our sizable market position and strategic manufacturer relationships to secure up to 10 gigawatts of incremental turbine capacity through 2035' — an option it is not committed to. CEO Bill Fehrman named the suppliers: 'using our size and scale and our relationships with namely GE Vernova and Mitsubishi to get this equipment locked up... we know that generation is going to be a driving force, and because of that, it's a scarce resource and will become increasingly more valuable.' Roughly half of the 13 GW already sits in the $78 billion plan; the other half rolls into the 2027-2031 plan. The 10 GW option is timed to replace aging coal and gas plants as they retire.
data.figure: Three gigawatts of turbines added in the quarter, taking total secured turbine capacity to approximately 13 GW through 2031; option on up to 10 GW more through 2035; about half of the 13 GW already inside the $78B plan

data.signal: TWO PROJECTS BEYOND THE BASE PLAN ARE MOVING TO DEFINITIVE AGREEMENTS AHEAD OF THE THIRD-QUARTER CAPITAL-PLAN REFRESH. Piketon (Ohio) transmission: AEP is 'working towards definitive agreements with the prospective offtaker, SP Energy', anticipates executed documents in the third quarter and would then roll the project into the 2027-2031 five-year plan; the company frames it as showcasing 'our industry-leading expertise in developing and operating 765 kV transmission infrastructure.' Wyoming fuel cells: at the contractual June 30 deadline AEP amended the agreement with the unnamed hyperscaler offtaker, modifying key protection terms so AEP is 'adequately compensated for their requested timing accommodations' while keeping the original December 2026 milestone intact, after which the hyperscaler may deploy the fuel cells at an alternate location if the Cheyenne, Wyoming site does not advance. Timing is gating: the fuel cells 'need to be installed and ready to go by the end of 2028 to qualify for the investment tax credit.'
data.figure: Piketon definitive agreements targeted for the third quarter with offtaker SP Energy; Wyoming fuel-cell December 2026 milestone intact, units must be installed by the end of 2028 to qualify for the investment tax credit
data.counterparty: SP Energy (Piketon transmission offtaker); unnamed hyperscaler (Wyoming fuel cells)

data.signal: LARGE-LOAD TARIFF FRAMEWORK NOW COVERS FIVE JURISDICTIONS — Virginia approved AEP's proposed large load tariff in June, 'bringing the total number of approved tariffs across the portfolio to five', with three additional filings pending. The tariffs 'require customers to make long-term commitments and support the investments necessary to serve their demand' and provide protections against project delays and changing development timelines. Because new large load signs take-or-pay electric service agreements, AEP projects fixed cost offsets for residential customers of up to $16 billion at its vertically integrated utilities — already flowing through as base rate reductions (an Ohio order received; Indiana Michigan Power to file a base rate decrease later this summer).
data.figure: Five large-load tariffs approved and three more filings pending; up to $16 billion of projected fixed-cost offsets for residential customers

data.signal: GENERATION ADDITIONS TO SERVE THE LOAD: Public Service Company of Oklahoma received a separate order in May approving its request to procure 1.3 gigawatts of generation resources; AEP has announced one West Virginia project of about 1.2 gigawatts with 'a number of other projects that are heading down the pathway' toward the governor's 50 by 50 target; and it is evaluating a GenCo structure alongside an early-stage nuclear strategy 'driven by demand from potential customers who value alternative forms of long-term baseload generation to support their rapidly growing demand', on fee-based arrangements with robust capital protection measures. AEP also buys existing generation into rate base for its vertically integrated utilities (projects purchased for Indiana Michigan Power) and offers behind-the-meter bridging power so customers get immediate capacity while transmission and generation are built.

data.signal: Six-inch indium phosphide ramp running ahead of plan: Coherent significantly increased InP production in Q2 and is on track to double internal InP production by the fourth quarter of calendar 2026. Current-quarter wafer starts are already at 80% of the doubling target, after wafer starts more than quadrupled from the September quarter to the December quarter; a wafer start takes about six months to become a transceiver shipment, so the benefit starts this quarter and builds over coming quarters. Production is ramping in parallel at Sherman, Texas and Yarfala, Sweden, with EMLs, CW lasers and photodiodes all in production on six-inch and six-inch yields exceeding three-inch yields. A six-inch wafer produces more than four times as many chips at less than half the cost; almost all capacity being added is six-inch, about half of capacity will be six-inch by the end of calendar 2026, and plans go well beyond doubling in following years. data.signal: CLOUD AI / DATA CENTER: CEO Rene Haas said data center royalty revenue 'has grown more than 100% year on year' and continues to double YoY. The drivers are the ramp of Arm-based chips at all major hyperscaler companies and 'ongoing share gains from custom hyperscaler chips'. The AI data-center build-out also lifts deployments of networking chips, particularly DPUs and smart NICs, where Arm says it has a very high market share. Arm expects its share among the top hyperscalers to reach 50%. Sizing (disclosed once a year): data center was double-digit % of revenue at the start of the year and should now be 'somewhere in kind of the teens to probably getting closer to 20%'. Over the next two to three years it should match or exceed the smartphone business, which is '40 to 45% of total business'. Haas: 'in a few years our data center business to be our largest business, larger than mobile'. Arm has reorganized into three business units: Edge AI (smartphone, IoT), Physical AI (automotive, robotics) and Cloud AI (data center, networking). In Physical AI, Rivian's third-generation autonomy computer is the first production vehicle on a custom Arm chip, and Tesla's upcoming Optimus humanoid robot is powered by a custom Arm-based AI processor.

data.signal: AGENTIC INFERENCE RAISES CPU CONTENT: AI is shifting from training to inference, and that inference is increasingly agent-based: 'persistent, always on, and power constrained'. Agent coordination runs on CPUs, so customers want higher core counts and better power efficiency. Haas said the latest hyperscaler and NVIDIA CPU generations 'have increased the number of cores. And we think that only continues.' He cited four examples. AWS's fifth-generation Graviton has 192 cores, double Graviton4. NVIDIA's Vera has 88 Arm-based cores, up from 72 cores in the 'gray CPU generation' (as transcribed). Microsoft's Cobalt 200 has 132 cores on Neoverse CSS V3, up from 128 in Cobalt 100 on Neoverse N2. Google previewed its second Arm server processor (Axion-powered m4a instances). Integrated platforms raise output per watt: AWS pairs Graviton with Arm-based Nitro DPUs and training accelerators, and NVIDIA pairs GPUs with Arm-based CPUs and BlueField. Over the next three years Haas expects CPUs to take on work GPUs used to do and more custom CPU-based chips to appear. He also sees specific prefill/decode inference solutions continuing to extend.
data.figure: Graviton 192 cores; Vera 88 cores (vs 72); Cobalt 200 132 cores (vs 128)

data.signal: COMPUTE SUBSYSTEMS (CSS): nearly two and a half years after launch, demand 'continues to exceed expectations'. Two more CSS licenses were signed in the quarter (Edge AI tablets and smartphones), for a total of 21 CSS licenses across 12 companies. Five customers now ship CSS-based chips, two of them on a second-generation platform, and the top four Android smartphone vendors ship CSS-powered devices. CSS was 'approaching double digit' of royalties last year and is 'into the teens' this year. Child said it 'could be upwards of 50%' over the next couple of years, and every CSS customer that could renew for the next generation has done so. Each smartphone cycle brings a new CSS, generally at a higher royalty rate. Haas sees no bill-of-materials pushback: fabs moving from five to three to two nanometer shorten design windows, so faster time to market is worth more than the cost. Neoverse CSS V3 underpins Microsoft's Cobalt 200.
data.figure: 21 CSS licenses across 12 companies; five customers shipping CSS chips; CSS royalty share into the teens, could be upwards of 50%

data.signal: MEMORY SHORTAGE vs SMARTPHONE ROYALTIES: Child noted that MediaTek talked about 'around a 15% reduction in unit volume for next year', in line with other handset makers' views on memory supply constraints. Partners are protecting the premium/flagship tier, where Arm's CSS and v9 royalties sit; the constraints should mostly hit the low end (v8 and older, with much smaller royalties). A 20% volume reduction would hit smartphone royalties by 'somewhere around a 2% or 4% at worst'. In a later answer he put it at 'at most a kind of four to 6%' within smartphones, already including contractually agreed higher per-unit rates. The effect on total royalties would be 'a 1%, maybe 2% negative impact', more than offset by cloud AI growing ahead of expectations. Memory impact on the Q4 guide is 'very minimal', and memory and other shortages affect Arm less than full-fab semiconductor companies. Haas added that Arm is highly involved in research on SRAM and alternative memory technologies for AI.
data.figure: 20% smartphone unit cut -> 2% or 4% at worst (at most four to 6%) smartphone royalty impact; 1%, maybe 2% on total royalties

data.signal: INVESTMENT / NEXT CATALYST: rising R&D spend funds next-generation architectures, compute subsystems and 'our exploration into chiplets and complete SoCs'. data.signal: CPO / ELSFP EXTERNAL LASER SOURCE ECONOMICS: ELSFP (external light source for co-packaged optics) is in very limited production now, ramping later in 2026 and through 2027 to ~400,000 PIECES PER MONTH IN 2028. Laser power scaling is the constraint: CPO/ELSFP uses a 300mW laser vs 70mW in an 800G transceiver and 100mW in a 1.6T transceiver, with die size ~6x larger, so meeting CPO demand requires the industry laser market to be 8-10x BIGGER than today; the next generation of ELSFP moves to DWDM, where yield loss is 40-50% worse than 1310nm. Laser capacity carries a 21-24 MONTH equipment-to-high-volume lead time. AOI is engaged with ~5 CPO customers on 3-4 year demand; several have already qualified AOI on fixed-wavelength CPO laser / ELSFP, with DWDM the current focus. High-volume ELSFP manufacturing is 'more like late Q3 next year' (late 2027). Houston laser fab capacity to grow ~300% by Q3 2027 plus a SECOND FAB cleanroom ~4x the size of the current facility (adding MOCVD, epi, steppers). Margin mix: laser gross margin 55-65%, ELSFP module ('EOSAP') >50%, both landing H2 2027. AOI is absent from first-generation CPO deployments purely because laser capacity must first feed AOI's own transceivers.
data.figure: ELSFP ~400k pcs/month in 2028; 300mW CPO laser vs 70mW(800G)/100mW(1.6T); industry laser capacity needs 8-10x; laser GM 55-65%

data.signal: BOTTLENECK HAS MOVED FROM LASERS TO DSP/TIA: because AOI makes its own lasers in-house it avoids the laser shortage that management calls 'the biggest bottleneck right now for the transceiver business' and 'the number one issue' for competitors; AOI's binding constraints for 800G/1.6T are instead DSP and TIA supply, where 'the whole supply chain is very tight' for 1.6T - AOI says its supplier ranks it FOURTH priority under a long-term partnership, with calls once or twice a week. INDIUM PHOSPHIDE SUBSTRATE: supply secured into end-2027 and 'incrementally better' than last quarter - not currently a limiter; AOI has just moved to 4-INCH substrate volume manufacturing and buys from 2 European + 2 Japanese + 3 Chinese suppliers, and is negotiating partnerships or a possible JOINT VENTURE with 2-3 of them for 2028-2029 volumes (laser capacity growing 'much more than a factor of 10'). Proprietary in-house production machinery insulates AOI from the industry's equipment-delivery bottlenecks.
data.figure: DSP/TIA = binding constraint (AOI ranked 4th priority); InP substrate secured to end-2027; 4-inch substrate volume production

Asked whether AOI is at about 200,000 units now heading to 650,000 by year end, he confirmed: 'Probably a little more than 200,000. We were 200,000 kind of at the end of last quarter', and AOI is 'on that pathway between 200 and 650'.

data.signal: SOLD OUT AND TURNING CUSTOMERS AWAY: Murry said that when another large data center customer asks for units today AOI has to answer that it is 'sold out at least through second half of next year and beyond'. Some large data center customers have already approached AOI ('some have') and it cannot take them without over-committing against existing customers; the only way in may be CPO or another newer technology further out. He confirmed the monthly data center transceiver target put to him is a REVENUE expectation, not merely a capacity figure, and said AOI could do more revenue than that if it had more capacity - 'the demand is not the limiting factor', capacity and to some extent supply chain are. Best case long-term share is 'somewhere around 20% market share'. Several LTAs are on the table but AOI is deliberately cautious: an LTA that locks up too much capacity for one customer could scare away other customers it wants later.
data.figure: sold out at least through second half of next year and beyond; somewhere around 20% market share

data.signal: WHERE THE 800G RAMP IS PHYSICALLY COMING FROM: Murry said 'two major hyperscale customers' are both buying meaningful 800G quantities with several smaller customers either buying or about to start. The step up from 'a few million dollars in 800G sales a quarter' to the Q3/Q4 projection comes MAINLY OUT OF THE TAIWAN PLANT - that is the capacity added this year. The Houston/US real estate starts only its very first increment later this year and is really a 2027 and into 2028 contributor.
data.figure: two major hyperscale customers; a few million dollars in 800G sales a quarter

data.signal: LASER FAB FOOTPRINT AND THE US PREMIUM: Murry said 'the lasers are only made here in the U.S.' in the Sugar Land facility, that AOI intends to add further laser production in the Houston area but does NOT intend to put laser production overseas, and that the added laser capacity lands mostly in the latter half of next year aimed at CPO/NPO devices. Asked whether customers pay up for that, he said flatly they are 'willing to pay a premium for U.S. production' - driven by the non-zero possibility of a ban on Chinese-sourced optics, which customers say would kill their ability to build new US data centers.
data.figure: the lasers are only made here in the U.S.; willing to pay a premium for U.S. production

data.signal: MEMORY SHORTAGE IS DRIVING THE 100G DECLINE (the Q2 FY2026 call already attributed the 100G weakness to the memory shortage; new here is the customer's allocation mechanism and the expedite-fee timing): Murry explained the unexpected margin headwind as 'one of our customers was unable to secure enough memory to meet all of their build-out needs', so that customer is reallocating the memory it can get to higher-speed nodes (800G, 1.6T) and deploying relatively fewer 100G links for the next few quarters - which hits AOI's high-margin 100G business. On expedite fees, he said the 1.6T volume came up faster than AOI's SUPPLIERS had planned for (they had discounted AOI's forecast and are now tight on capacity), but that this irons itself out over the next few months and should not be much of a factor beyond Q4.
data.figure: one of our customers was unable to secure enough memory to meet all of their build-out needs

data.signal: CPO PIPELINE AND CPO MARGIN STRUCTURE: Murry said AOI has 'five companies' it is talking to about CPO, some of which are also in real NPO discussions, and expects MORE THAN ONE CPO customer - but probably not all five, because it will not have enough capacity for everyone. On economics, CPO ELSFP or laser-diode margins 'should be meaningfully above 40%', with the bare laser chip 'most likely above 60%' and modules in between, so CPO/NPO mix can pull group margin above the 40% long-term target once it scales.
data.figure: five companies; margins should be meaningfully above 40%; most likely above 60%

data.signal: SCALE-UP LASER CONTENT - THE INDUSTRY CAPACITY GAP QUANTIFIED: Murry agreed scale-up optics is 'an order of magnitude-ish increase' in the NUMBER of lasers per rack versus scale-out, and added the die itself is 'five or six times larger size per laser', so the wafer real estate the industry must process rises enormously. He said there is not enough capacity in the industry right now to come close to meeting scale-up demand, let alone scale-out - which is why AOI and its competitors are all investing in laser fabs. He called the AI shift in optics the most impactful game changer he has seen in 30 years in the business.
data.figure: an order of magnitude-ish increase; five or six times larger size per laser

data.signal: WAFER SIZE AND SUBSTRATE SUPPLY: AOI runs lasers on four-inch wafers today; all fab equipment bought in the last year or two can go to six-inch and AOI will switch only when six-inch is cheaper per laser than four-inch and six-inch substrate availability exists - no date is set in stone. On substrates, Murry said AOI feels good about availability through next year, through 2027, and is actively working with a number of vendors to secure 2028-and-beyond capacity; substrate pricing 'has gone up a little bit' but is not a dramatic margin impact, and laser yields still have room to improve, which can offset the higher substrate cost.
data.figure: We are a four-inch right now; pricing has gone up a little bit

data.signal: CAPEX PAYBACK AND FUNDING MIX: CFO/CSO Stefan Murry said capex goes almost entirely into production equipment, machinery and the supporting real estate, and 'most of the investments that we’re making are 9 to 10 months ROI'. He listed four funding routes: equity (leaned on now, but it 'will become less a factor for us in the future'), cash from operations, a customer contribution ('there are still discussions ongoing about what that could look like'), and less- or non-dilutive debt structures, and said AOI is also 'seeing some government subsidy income'. He argued a U.S. move against Chinese competitors could come with government investment to speed up U.S. industry, and that 'raising everything on the back of equity for the foreseeable future is not our plan.'
data.figure: 9 to 10 months ROI

data.signal: LRO READY, LPO NOT FULLY PRODUCTIZED, CUSTOMERS STILL BUY FULL DSP: Murry said 'we do have LRO products for sure. We have some designs on LPO. I wouldn’t say they’re productized completely at this point.' The production process is built to switch readily between types, though moving away from DSPs depends on sourcing the replacement components, and 'customers by and large, are still demanding full DSP solutions at this point.'

data.signal: Q4 FY2025 HEADLINE RESULTS: record revenue of $134,300,000, +34% year over year and +13% sequentially, in line with the $125,000,000 to $140,000,000 guidance; non-GAAP gross margin 31.4% (above the 29% to 31% guide, up from 31% in Q3 2025 and 28.9% a year ago, on favorable mix and cost reduction); non-GAAP loss per share $0.01 vs a guided loss of $0.13 to $0.04; non-GAAP operating loss $7,100,000; GAAP net loss $2,000,000. Revenue mix: 56% data center, 40% CATV, 4% FTTH/telecom/other. Full-year 2025 revenue rose 83% to a record $456,000,000 with CATV revenue nearly tripling to $245,000,000. Revenue is net of warrant contra revenue (approximately 2.5% of revenue from warrant-holding customers; $730,000 in Q4).

DATA CENTER SPEED MIX: Q4 data center revenue $74,900,000, up 69% year over year and 70% sequentially. 100G sales +54% Y/Y and 400G sales +141% Y/Y. Data center revenue split: 51% 100G, 41% 200G/400G, 8% 10G/40G. 800G revenue came in below the $4,000,000 to $8,000,000 expectation because of ongoing firmware optimization at the hyperscale customer - CFO Stefan Murry said it was 'a bit below $4,000,000' - but strength in 400G with that customer more than offset it. Q1 data center growth expected to come principally from continued 400G growth plus some 800G.

800G RAMP TIMING: during Q4 AOI received an 800G volume order from one of its major hyperscale customers after that customer qualified AOI's 800G products (the CFO called it the 'first 800G volume order'; the CEO's turn as printed says 'fourth'). The remaining hurdle is firmware interoperability across the customer's many switch platforms ('Hardware-wise, everything is fine'), agreed to be finished around mid-March; AOI had expected a green light to ship in December. It describes the architectural evolution as pluggable transceivers with DSPs, to LPO platforms that remove the DSP, morphing into smaller package-less NPO platforms; those architectures still need drivers and TIAs, but with much higher density - smaller parts, more channels, lower power, and varied form factors using wire bonds, bumped devices or flip chip, plus through-silicon-via options. Because these solutions are specific to the architectures hyperscalers are driving, the design wins come directly to MACOM. Related applications include LPO and LRO on single mode or multimode.

data.signal: WHY MI450 RUNS UALINK OVER ETHERNET, AND WHAT IT MEANS FOR ASTERA CONTENT: asked about the first Helios server, CEO Jitendra Mohan declined to speak for AMD but reiterated AMD's public position - 'for the MI450 series, they are going to go with UALink running over Ethernet. That has really got everything to do with the fact that UALink switches are not yet available', so MI450 must tunnel UALink over Ethernet - while AMD has said it will keep offering both UALink over Ethernet and native UALink in future generations, which Mohan expects to coexist. The content consequence he spelled out generically: where Astera does not supply the scale-up switching, its content is limited to scale-out retimers, Scorpio P, Taurus Ethernet retimers and active electrical cables; where the scale-up protocol is one Astera supports (PCI Express, UALink or something in between) and a Scorpio X solution can be used, 'then our content really does explode a lot, because scale up is a very rich area for connectivity solutions'. He added that the in-network compute, Hypercast, diagnostics and telemetry built into today's Scorpio X, exposed through COSMOS software, carry forward to a UALink-based Scorpio X, making the migration easy for existing Scorpio X users.

data.signal: AI test intensity is compounding because design margins are shrinking: higher data rates, lower latency and the requirement that AI fabrics be LOSSLESS mean customers 'can no longer guarantee anything by design' and must test in production too. A compute or switch tray has gone from tens to HUNDREDS of IC pinouts - more insertion points - tested at signal level (VNAs, oscilloscopes), at bit level (new portfolio) and at protocol/packet level (AI workload emulators). The move from monolithic chips to CHIPLET architectures adds interoperability emulation, and customers now ask for emulation environments that stress a chip while it exercises a model (thermal shutdown, all cores active at higher power and speed). The ecosystem is shifting from a homogeneous integrated vertical stack to a HETEROGENEOUS one - GPU/CPU/DPU mixes and a growing number of protocols at every layer of the stack - which broadens Keysight's addressable tail. The four wireline pillars (AI infrastructure scaling, speed transitions, silicon photonics, system-level emulation) all drove growth. Hyperscaler engagement (rooted in the Ixia acquisition ~5 years ago) is deepening as they integrate Keysight pre-silicon emulation and workload solutions into their development pipelines; hyperscalers plus the model companies are ~10% OF REVENUE DIRECTLY but drive large downstream influence, and many are building their own in-house silicon. Switch designers use Keysight emulators to validate network performance across AI workloads and protocols; interconnect manufacturers use high-fidelity analyzers to characterize high-speed backplanes for signal integrity and manufacturing yield.
data.figure: Hundreds of IC pinouts per tray; hyperscalers ~10% of revenue direct; chiplet + workload emulation

Content per test is also rising: 400G was laser/dispersion/power in-out, 800G adds precise laser and insertion-loss measurement, and 'as you go to 1.6T, it is a whole new ballgame... a lot more functional test on the line'. data.signal: CPO TEST - TIMING AND WHERE VIAVI SITS: Khaykin said Viavi has been working on a CPO test 'now for well over 12 to close to 2 years. We are now started shipping, I would say even this quarter is early shipments.' Test capacity is facilitized ahead of demand and the next increment is added at about '60%, 70% utilization'. CPO pulls Viavi into semiconductor test next to Advantest, Teradyne and FormFactor - the configuration is an IC tester plus a prober plus an optical rack, all interconnected - and he expects a HIGHER share for Viavi there than in pluggables because Viavi sells an automatable integrated platform with '2,500 SKUs' of measurement modules rather than a point solution. Content per port rises sharply: pluggable is power, dispersion and insertion loss, CPO is multiple insertions plus extensive functional test, with known-good-die, optical-engine and interconnect-platform insertions all before the ASIC and memory go on a module worth 'thousands of dollars' - skip them and 'you will be throwing away tens of millions of dollars'.

Because the cost of one bad port pair is a bad switch, customers 'test everything to the nth degree', and for a '100 terabit switch, I don't think anybody's going to skip any tests'.

data.signal: Copper versus optical: management insists it is 'copper AND optical.' Copper stays the workhorse inside the rack and in scale-up, and the shift to agentic workloads deploys MORE CPUs and networking, which increases the addressable market for high-speed copper connectivity. Scale-out is already almost entirely optical and TE openly states it has only a limited position there. The inflection management sees as incremental upside is CPO arriving at the switch level, which is where TE's fiber-array-unit technology plugs into its connectivity suite as incremental TAM rather than a substitution risk.
data.figure: no specific figure

data.signal: Optical roadmap via the RAM Photonics acquisition: TE added fiber-attached connectivity (FAU, fiber array unit) capability and says customer engagement around it is strong, opening incremental market access as optics move off the switch in scale-out architectures. Management was explicit on timing - 'you won't really see meaningful revenue until we get to 2028 and beyond' - and is currently investing in scaling both the manufacturing and the engineering teams from that acquisition to hit the customer intercept point in the 2028+ timeframe.
data.figure: FAU/optical meaningful revenue not until 2028 and beyond

data.signal: Power connectivity is roughly ONE THIRD of TE's AI revenue, with data connectivity the other two thirds. As customers move to higher-voltage rack architectures (some experimenting with 800V, though management sees a continuum of trade-offs rather than one end game), TE says content can rise to about 1.5x traditional power content. Curtin does not expect new entrants, because the rack is 'a simultaneous equation of trade-offs and constraints between the data and the power equation' and customers value a supplier that understands both the power chain and the signal chain. Introducing optics itself creates more power need.
data.figure: ~1/3 of AI revenue is power connectivity; higher-voltage architectures worth ~1.5x traditional power content

data.signal: Energy business organic sales grew 33%, contributing well over $100 million of the quarter's roughly $600 million of total growth. In recent weeks Ciena FINALIZED LONG-TERM AGREEMENTS that secure supply of certain key components THROUGH 2029, including incremental capacity for those key components; the June five-year zero-coupon convertible (economic conversion premium of 114%, proceeds retiring the 5.5% interest term loan) partly provided the capital to help secure supply over the next three years, and cash from operations will step down in Q4 as those investments are dispersed. Ciena is also qualifying additional suppliers — expanding both the number of suppliers and alternative technologies for the same functionality. Capital investments this year increased capacity sufficient to support RLS, plug and Waveserver revenue growth all over 60% year to date; capex expected at the high end of the $250 million-$275 million range; $2.8 billion in cash and equivalents. Value exchange with customers: price increases from high single digits up to high teens/low 20s depending on customer and product line, some of it selectively hitting backlog, alongside payment-terms and fill-rate discussions; possible new Canadian tariff impact of ~$10 million a quarter being mitigated.

data.signal: AI portfolio catalysts: WaveLogic 6 Extreme — after 18 months still the ONLY 1.6 Tb high-performance modem on the market — with a ramp already exceeding WaveLogic 5 Extreme and output doubled. RLS holds roughly 70% market share in disaggregated optical line systems; next-generation RLS HYPER-RAIL (co-created with the hyperscalers for scale-across / distributed AI training over greater distances) is on track for initial customer standardization by the end of calendar 2026 and will ramp to SEVERAL HUNDRED MILLION DOLLARS of revenue in 2027 (could be faster with more components), with economics a step function above RLS and accretive to corporate average margins. Interconnects: Q3 800 ZR pluggable shipments MORE THAN TWICE the previous quarter's volume; strong market receptivity to Nitro, the linear redriver for active copper cable solutions; VESTA, the open co-packaged optics (CPX) solution, received SAMPLE ORDERS FROM SEVERAL ANCHOR CUSTOMERS in the ecosystem — CPX revenue expected to begin in 2027 and ramp into 2028. Coherent moving inside the data center is viewed as inevitable with the right general-market intercept at 3.2 Tb; OCS is welcomed as driving coherent adoption inside the data center faster (no comment on Ciena entering the OCS market itself). The major-hyperscaler WaveLogic 6 Extreme win announced last quarter — DSP, drivers, TIAs and coherent expertise in a complete module deployed across the customer's own global optical platform, a significant takeaway from a component competitor — is one of two bespoke performance-optics consumption-model relationships. TAM expected to effectively double from approximately $25 billion today to approximately $50 billion by 2029; scale-across is a major demand driver, almost entirely North American/US-based and just beginning, with asynchronous training and inference traffic still ahead.

The structure the hyperscalers 'seem to be okay with' is 'a very heavy capacity payment' plus a variable component that 'turns into basically a heat rate for the hyperscaler. They take the gas risk.' data.signal: Data center pricing and returns (President/CFO): the price target was adjusted 'to an $80-plus kind of range', but building '1.2 gigawatts of GEV turbines' puts the price at the high end: 'think north of the $90 to $95 range where we were back in our original guidance.' Because the deals are very heavy on capacity, that value does not map cleanly to a $/MWh price. Deals on NRG sites also involve a land transaction that is not in that number. NRG gets its return and capital back inside the 20-year contract and is 'one of the few people who've got 9 turbines that people can go put on the ground'. Every project must clear the 12% to 15% pretax unlevered hurdle rate. data.signal: Component shortages were the quarter's defining constraint. Because plants were already being staffed and prepared for significantly higher volume, the part shortages caused temporary downtime and lower-than-planned capacity utilisation across the expansion sites: excess labour plus unfavourable overhead absorption on the lower volumes had a 450-550 basis point impact on Data Center margin in the quarter, on top of a 150 basis point year-over-year warranty variance from a large prior-year settlement. Modine repositioned available parts to its highest-producing, most efficient lines and idled others, and rationed supply so that its largest key accounts got priority over smaller customers. By the third month of the quarter (June) Data Center margin was 'right back where we'd expect it to be,' and management said it has now secured the supply chain needed to meet demand for the rest of the year.

data.signal: Data center pipeline: over 48 gigawatts in various stages of contracting as of December 2025 versus around 47 gigawatts as of September, an increase of approximately 1.4 gigawatts or 3% (split into substation engineering letters of authorization, construction letters of authorization and electrical service agreements). The demand forecast is validated by 20-plus gigawatts of signed ESA and CLOA contracts, and forecasted data center demand through 2045 is more than covered by existing signed ESAs and CLOAs (nothing is forecast from SELOAs). The vast majority of demand growth is driven by steady and consistent batches of cloud and inference data center modules, limiting reliance on any single project or customer. Starting in January 2027, large load customers with demand of 25 megawatts or greater face minimum demand charges, and new ESAs carry firm contract terms with exit fees and enhanced collateral. Virginia data center load has grown at a 20% CAGR since 2016 while residential rates averaged 9% below the national average. Other large customers are not being crowded out, and on a Virginia Senate proposal that could remove a data center tax benefit, management said the outcome is hard to predict but it expects data center growth to continue.

data.signal: Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind is over 70% complete and on track to deliver first power to the grid by March: all 176 monopiles were installed faster than expected, the third and final offshore substation is installed, and deepwater export cables are in; around 70% of towers and nacelles and 30% of blades are fabricated; the first turbine was completed in January. Management argues existing and new supply are not bifurcated: even a customer that self-manages peaks via Connect and Manage 'will still need to buy energy for all of the other hours', which is where the existing fixed-price, carbon-free nuclear fleet becomes the multi-decade product customers want.
